Pregnancy

Induction of labour: benefits, risks and newborn care

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Induction starts labour medically before it begins on its own. It can protect a pregnant person or baby when continuing pregnancy carries greater risk, but it also brings choices about procedures, monitoring and pain relief. The useful comparison is induction now versus a specific plan for waiting: not induction versus an imagined birth without any complications.

What induction involves

Induction may begin with medicines or a mechanical method, such as a balloon catheter, to soften and open the cervix. Breaking the waters and an oxytocin infusion may follow when appropriate. The sequence depends on the cervix, the baby's position, previous births and medical history; not everyone needs every step.

Induction is different from augmentation, which strengthens labour that has already started. Both can involve oxytocin, but the reasons and circumstances differ. Ask which method is proposed, what it is intended to do, how you and your baby will be monitored and what happens if it does not work.

When starting labour may be safer than waiting

Reasons can include a pregnancy continuing beyond its due date, waters breaking before labour, or a condition affecting the pregnant person or baby. For an uncomplicated pregnancy, NICE recommends discussing induction from 41 weeks because some risks increase as pregnancy continues. This is a discussion about the individual's situation and local guidance, not a date that makes every pregnancy identical.

Diabetes, high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia can change the balance, but a diagnosis alone does not mean everyone must have the same induction at the same week. Severity, treatment, growth and wellbeing matter. Sometimes prompt birth is needed, and sometimes cesarean birth is the safer route. Ask why birth is recommended now and what could happen with a defined period of waiting.

Timing matters for the baby

Preterm birth is before 37 completed weeks; 37 weeks through 38 weeks and 6 days is early term, and 39 through 40 weeks and 6 days is full term. These distinctions matter because breathing, feeding and temperature control may still be immature. Elective delivery without a medical reason should not be confused with necessary early delivery.

Waiting until 39 weeks is not a rule that overrides a serious maternal or fetal problem. When early birth is advised, ask about the risks of staying pregnant, the baby's likely support needs and whether a neonatal team should be involved. Decisions use the best available pregnancy dating and the current clinical picture.

Contractions, monitoring and a previous cesarean

Medicines used for induction can cause contractions that are too frequent or too prolonged. This can affect the baby's heart rate. Monitoring helps the team recognize a problem; depending on the method, they may stop the medicine, remove a removable vaginal preparation, give treatment to relax the uterus or expedite birth. A mechanical method has a different risk profile but is not risk-free.

A previous cesarean or other uterine surgery changes the choice of method because the uterine scar can rupture. Some induction medicines are unsuitable after a cesarean. Tell the team about every uterine operation and ask about the individual options, including planned cesarean birth. Do not try to induce labour with medicines, herbs or devices at home.

Pain relief and assisted vaginal birth

Induced labour can feel more painful, and cervical preparation and repeated assessments can be tiring. Available pain relief should be discussed before starting and reviewed as labour changes. Options may include simple comfort measures, medicines and an epidural, depending on your situation and the setting. Needing pain relief is not a failure.

Monitoring or an infusion can affect mobility and where you give birth. Forceps or vacuum assistance and perineal tears are possible outcomes of childbirth, but induction does not create an inevitable chain from epidural to assisted birth or severe tearing. Personal factors, the reason for induction and the course of labour matter; ask about support for movement and your preferences.

Does induction increase cesarean birth?

There is no single answer for every pregnancy. The 2018 ARRIVE trial studied low-risk people having their first birth, with one head-down baby and reliable dating. Induction at 39 weeks resulted in cesarean birth in 18.6%, compared with 22.2% with expectant management. Waiting in that trial could still lead to a later induction; it did not mean everyone went into labour spontaneously.

The trial did not find a statistically significant reduction in its primary combined measure of serious newborn outcomes. Its findings do not promise the same result for twins, a previous cesarean, a medical complication or an earlier gestation, and do not rule out rare harms. Discuss evidence that fits your circumstances rather than assuming induction always raises (or always lowers) your chance of surgery.

If induction takes time or does not succeed

Cervical preparation and labour can take many hours, sometimes longer than a day. Slow progress does not by itself prove that anyone has done something wrong. Ask how progress will be assessed, when the plan will be reviewed and what support, food, rest or company is possible under local arrangements.

If induction is unsuccessful, the team reassesses you and the baby. Depending on safety and preferences, options can include a rest period, another attempt, waiting with an agreed plan or cesarean birth. If either of you is unwell, waiting may no longer be appropriate. A revised plan should explain both the reason and its urgency.

Breathing, feeding and neonatal admission

A baby born early or affected by an underlying condition may need help with breathing, feeding, keeping warm or other problems. Admission to a neonatal unit after induction does not by itself show that induction caused the problem: the gestation and the reason for delivery can be central. Nor does induction mean a baby will automatically need special care.

If admission is possible, ask what care may be needed and how parents can participate. Touch, holding or skin-to-skin contact depend on the baby's condition; expressing milk may help when direct feeding is not yet possible. Separation and an unexpected change of plan can be distressing. Ask for practical and emotional support and clear updates from the neonatal team.

Jaundice and the question about oxytocin

Jaundice is yellowing caused by a build-up of bilirubin, produced as red blood cells break down. Newborns may not clear it efficiently yet; this does not mean their red blood cells cannot carry oxygen. Feeding difficulties and other conditions can also matter. A suspected case needs assessment and, when indicated, a bilirubin measurement rather than a judgement based only on skin colour.

Jaundice after an induced birth is not proof that oxytocin caused it. Associations are difficult to separate from gestation, feeding and the circumstances of birth. In ARRIVE, 4.7% of babies in each group received treatment for raised bilirubin; that trial was not a comparison of oxytocin doses. Do not use an online dose threshold to make treatment decisions. Feeding support and sometimes phototherapy are based on the baby's assessment.

When to seek help

Before or during a planned induction, contact the maternity team immediately for reduced or changed fetal movements, leaking waters, bleeding, fever, severe headache or visual changes. Tell staff immediately if you feel unwell during the procedure. Get emergency help for heavy bleeding or collapse, or if bleeding is accompanied by severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, feeling faint, dizziness or loss of consciousness. Any one of these warning signs is enough; do not wait for a booked induction appointment.

For a newborn, jaundice in the first 24 hours needs emergency assessment. Also seek emergency help if a jaundiced baby is sleepier than usual or difficult to wake; is not feeding; is floppy or stiff, or has jerking or twitching movements; has a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, feels hot or cold, or is shivering; has no wet nappies; or has difficulty breathing or is breathing very fast. Any one of these signs is enough; they do not all need to be present. New or worsening jaundice after 24 hours, dark urine or pale stools also needs urgent medical advice. The maternity or newborn team should explain how to obtain help locally and what follow-up is planned.

Questions that make the decision clearer

Ask: What is the reason for birth now? What are the benefits and risks of waiting, and how would we monitor that? Which method fits my history and cervix? What pain relief is available? What would make us stop, try another method or recommend cesarean birth? Ask for absolute numbers when useful and for an explanation of uncertainty.

Your preferences, previous experiences and concerns belong in the plan. You can ask for time to discuss options when the situation permits, or reconsider a choice as circumstances change. Declining or delaying induction should lead to a clear discussion of risks and an agreed care plan, rather than leaving you without support. Urgent clinical problems may limit how long it is safe to wait.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Recommendations depend on the clinical situation and local maternity services.

ARRIVE applies to a selected low-risk first-birth population; its findings are not universal guarantees.

Historical study and page dates are retained; evidence was checked in November 2026.

When to seek help

This article is educational and cannot choose a birth plan for you. Follow your maternity team's individualized advice and seek urgent or emergency help for the warning signs described.

Key takeaways

  • Compare induction with a realistic, monitored waiting plan.
  • Timing, the indication, the method and a uterine scar affect the balance of risks.
  • Induction does not invariably increase cesarean or assisted birth.
  • Newborn problems may reflect gestation or illness, rather than induction alone.
  • Know the maternity and newborn warning signs and how to get help.

Frequently asked questions

What does induction of labour mean?

It means medically starting labour before it begins on its own. Cervical medicines or a balloon, breaking the waters and oxytocin may be used in different sequences. Strengthening labour that has already started is called augmentation.

Is induction wrong or unnecessarily risky?

No. It can reduce the risks of continuing a pregnancy when there is a good indication. It also has possible harms and practical consequences. The decision compares induction at a particular time with an explicit waiting plan, taking your health, the baby and your preferences into account.

Does induction always lead to a cesarean?

No. Many induced labours end in vaginal birth. In the selected low-risk first-birth population in ARRIVE, 39-week induction reduced cesarean births compared with expectant management. That result is not a guarantee or a rule for every pregnancy.

Must every person with diabetes or pre-eclampsia be induced?

No single timing or method suits everyone. The condition's severity and the health of the pregnant person and baby determine when and how birth is recommended. Some situations need prompt delivery or a cesarean instead of induction.

Will I need an epidural or an assisted birth?

Neither is inevitable. Discuss pain relief before induction and ask again as needs change. An epidural is one option. Assisted birth depends on the circumstances of labour; a simple chain from induction to epidural to severe tearing is misleading.

Does oxytocin cause jaundice in every newborn?

No. Newborn jaundice has several contributing factors, and occurring after induction does not establish the cause. ARRIVE found the same proportion treated for raised bilirubin in both groups, but did not test oxytocin dosing. A jaundiced baby needs appropriate assessment, not assumptions about the birth.

What if induction does not work?

The team checks you and the baby, then discusses a pause, another attempt, a waiting plan or cesarean birth as appropriate. Urgent maternal or fetal concerns can change the options. Ask when reassessment will happen and what would make the plan change sooner.

Does early birth mean induction should always be avoided?

No. Before 39 weeks the baby's maturity is an important consideration, but continuing a pregnancy can sometimes be more dangerous. Ask about the specific reason for early delivery and the expected newborn care. Never postpone an urgent recommendation solely to reach a calendar milestone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
